Osteoarthritis

pharmacotherapy ladder · class right, member wrong · ketorolac's 5-day maximum · excluding inflammatory arthritisIs the offered drug the right member of the right class for a chronic condition in this patient?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Older adult, pain in a weight-bearing joint after use that rest relieves, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus, no fever osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease)
  • Exercise and weight loss first; a topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) for the knee or hand, an oral NSAID next; acetaminophen only when NSAIDs cannot be taken
  • Right class, wrong member: ketorolac stops at 5 days, so it never treats a chronic joint; there is generally no role for oral glucocorticoids, and none for hydroxychloroquine or methotrexate
What it is

The most common arthritis: progressive loss of joint cartilage with bony overgrowth, a mechanical rather than inflammatory joint disease

Driver

Activated chondrocytes release matrix metalloproteinases and cytokines that break down the cartilage matrix

Triggers

Age over 60 (non-modifiable)

Obesity

Joint trauma

Female sex (non-modifiable)

An earlier deformity of the joint, such as Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease or avascular necrosis of the scaphoid (non-modifiable)

Chain

Molecular: chondrocyte enzymes and cytokines cartilage matrix breaks down

Structural: joint space narrows osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts bone polishes on bone (eburnation)

Clinical: pain after use, worse by evening brief stiffness crepitus and lost range of motion

Insights

The pattern is mechanical, so oral steroids and disease-modifying drugs miss: no fever, no long stiffness, no synovitis, and joint fluid usually under 2,000 white cells

Topical comes first because the knee and hand are superficial: the drug may reach the joint with limited systemic exposure, which matters most in older patients

2Urgent risks
Hot, swollen jointA single red, swollen, painful joint, usually the knee, developing over hours or days

If a joint is warm with an effusion, choose arthrocentesis first: septic arthritis must be excluded.

NSAID harm in an older patientGastrointestinal bleeding, kidney injury and cardiovascular events

If there is kidney injury or insufficiency, or a prior gastrointestinal bleed, choose a topical NSAID or acetaminophen rather than a systemic NSAID, which may be contraindicated. Why not ketorolacThe label limits ketorolac to 5 days in all, for moderately severe acute pain. It is contraindicated after a gastrointestinal bleed or peptic ulcer and in advanced kidney disease, it inhibits platelets, and older patients carry more gastrointestinal risk.

3Differential
Chronic joint pain in an adult, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease)Knees, where wear begins medially, hips and lower spine; distal and proximal interphalangeal (DIP, PIP) and first carpometacarpal (CMC) joints; asymmetricGradual onset, chronic and progressive; stiffness under 30 minutes; Heberden and Bouchard nodes; spares the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints
Rheumatoid arthritisSymmetric MCP and PIP synovitis with fatigue or feverMorning stiffness over an hour; anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibody; erosions and periarticular osteopenia
Septic arthritis
One red, hot, swollen joint, usually the kneeHours to days; joint fluid over 50,000 white cells
Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease)Flares in a degenerated joint, most often the kneeAcute flares; rhomboid, weakly positive birefringent crystals; chondrocalcinosis on the radiograph
Hemochromatosis arthropathySecond and third MCP jointsHook-like osteophytes; high ferritin and transferrin saturation
Medial meniscal tearKnee pain with a small effusionLocking or catching
Patellofemoral pain syndromePain around or behind the patellaPain on quadriceps contraction against the patella (grind test)

Spine osteoarthritis is the usual cause of spinal stenosis; hip osteoarthritis can mimic trochanteric pain.

4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Months of knee pain in a 72-year-old; the only NSAID offered is ketorolacRight class, wrong member: a 5-day drugAcetaminophen, when no other NSAID is among the options
Kidney injury or insufficiency, or a prior gastrointestinal bleedAvoid a systemic NSAIDA topical NSAID or acetaminophen
Body mass index 35Weight loss is the highest-value stepWeight loss with exercise
Morning stiffness over an hour with symmetric MCP synovitisRheumatoid arthritis, not osteoarthritisRheumatoid factor and anti-CCP; disease-modifying drugs
Pause point
Chronic joint pain, NSAID chosen Offered: ketorolac Right class, wrong member → Not ketorolac for a chronic joint
A joint with no inflammation Offered: an oral steroid or hydroxychloroquine No inflammation → No oral steroid or hydroxychloroquine
5Diagnostic criteria
Clinical diagnosis, confirmed by radiograph Who – older adult, risk highest over 60 · Pain – weight-bearing joint, worse with use, eased by rest · Stiffness – under 30 minutes, easing with movement · Exam – bony enlargement, crepitus, less range of motion · Radiograph – LOSS: the joint space narrows, osteophytes form, and the bone under the cartilage turns sclerotic and cystic
6Severity
What raises the stakes
FindingMeansDo
Older age or heart diseaseHigher NSAID riskTopical first; lowest oral dose for the shortest time, with gastric protection considered
Kidney injury or insufficiency, or a prior bleedA systemic NSAID may be contraindicatedA topical NSAID or acetaminophen
Pain despite exercise, weight loss and NSAIDsSevere diseaseIntra-articular glucocorticoid Intra-articular glucocorticoidIntra-articular glucocorticoids give short-term relief; frequent injections may speed cartilage loss.
End-stage joint, all conservative measures failedRefractory diseaseTotal joint replacement
7Treatment
1

Alwaysevery patient

Exercise, with quadriceps strengthening for the knee; weight loss when overweight; a self-management program
2

First drugknee or hand

Topical NSAID, such as diclofenac Hip osteoarthritisA hip joint lies deep, so a topical NSAID is unlikely to help, and hip or many-joint disease starts with an oral NSAID. Hip pain is felt in the groin (likely the most specific site), sometimes at the greater trochanter or referred to the thigh and knee.
3

Raisepain persists, or the hip or many joints

Oral NSAID at the lowest dose for the shortest time; a proton pump inhibitor if gastrointestinal risk
4

If NSAIDs cannot be takenintolerance or contraindication

Acetaminophen, short-term; duloxetine, a serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; topical capsaicin for the knee AcetaminophenIn practice: the 2019 American College of Rheumatology guideline keeps topical NSAIDs for the knee and oral NSAIDs strongly recommended and lists acetaminophen only conditionally, for short-term use when NSAIDs cannot be taken, because its trial effects are very small. Older board items still key acetaminophen.
5

Injectsevere pain despite the above

Intra-articular glucocorticoid
6

Replacerefractory, end-stage joint

Total joint replacement
Not on the ladder
DrugWhy not
KetorolacA 5-day limit, for acute pain only
Oral glucocorticoidsNo role; the steroid route in osteoarthritis is intra-articular
Hydroxychloroquine, methotrexateStrongly recommended against: no inflammation to treat
Glucosamine, bisphosphonatesStrongly recommended against
OpioidsFew benefits and high risk; the American College of Rheumatology guideline allows tramadol only as a conditional recommendation
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
On an oral NSAIDWatch for gastrointestinal, cardiovascular and kidney effects
On a long-term NSAIDGastric protection
On repeated injectionsSpace them: frequent injections may speed cartilage loss
Pain despite every nonsurgical stepRefer for joint replacement
Practice
  1. 68 yo F with knee osteoarthritis still limited by pain despite exercise and weight loss → Topical diclofenac → the first-line drug for knee OA
  2. Knee OA with chronic kidney disease or prior GI bleed → Topical NSAID or acetaminophen, avoid systemic NSAIDs
  3. Refractory pain despite NSAIDs and physical therapy → Intra-articular glucocorticoid
  4. Morning stiffness >1 hour with symmetric metacarpophalangeal/proximal interphalangeal synovitis → Rheumatoid arthritis → rheumatoid factor/anti-CCP, DMARDs
  5. Acute monoarticular knee with warmth and effusion → Arthrocentesis before any pharmacotherapy
  6. End-stage disease, failed all conservative measures → Joint replacement
Transferable rule When choosing initial pharmacotherapy, read which specific agent represents each class. A class can be right while the offered member is wrong: ketorolac for chronic OA (osteoarthritis), gentamicin for simple cystitis, chloramphenicol for otitis. Check the offered drug rather than rejecting the guideline.
